column4: This ayah promises mercy to those who fear God, pay zakat, and believe; the next ayah calls its followers successful, making the section's link between a given share and success explicit across the passage.

This ayah concludes that followers of the Messenger are successful; 7:156 immediately before it names paying zakat among the traits of those promised mercy, joining the image's given share to falah while each verse contributes a distinct part.

The section develops تَزَكَّىٰ as self-purification through growth and giving; Moses uses the same verb when he asks Pharaoh whether he will purify himself, offering another Quranic setting for the section's central action.

The section interprets tazkiya as a wealth share given to purify; this ayah defines righteousness through giving wealth to named recipients, prayer, and zakat, specifying the ethical acts behind that purification.

The section says the crop's given share cleans what remains; this ayah warns that reproach and harm can nullify charity, comparing such spending to soil washed from bare rock, a failed counterpart to fruitful giving.

The section contrasts tended ground and a field whose growth is lost; this ayah describes a corrupt person striving to destroy crops and offspring, making deliberate destruction the field's moral opposite.

The section links a crop's fate to whether its yield is rightly cultivated and shared; this ayah compares what wrongdoers spend to a freezing wind that strikes and destroys a people's harvest, showing spending that yields no good.

The section contrasts a productive field with ground whose growth fails; this ayah says good soil yields plants by its Lord's leave while bad soil yields little, making soil and care visible in the difference of outcome.
The section explains zakat as a share given from wealth; this ayah assigns the alms to the poor, needy, collectors, and other named recipients, specifying who may receive that share.
The section connects a given share to falah; this ayah commands spending for one's own good and says those protected from the soul's stinginess are successful, linking release of wealth with success.
The section's harvest due is a share that leaves the yield for others; this ayah shows the righteous giving food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite their own desire for it.

The givers say they seek God's face and no repayment or thanks; this continuation specifies the intention behind 76:8's food-sharing, clarifying that the section's given share is not a transaction for return.

The section contrasts a worldly field with an afterlife field; this ayah says to seek the Hereafter with what God has given while not forgetting one's worldly share, making the two uses of provision explicit.
The section's root ب ق ي names what remains after yield and what endures; this ayah states that all on earth perishes, setting the contrast that the next ayah completes.
This ayah says the face of the Lord remains; after 55:26's perishing earth, it gives a Quranic form of endurance beyond the section's passing crop and lasting Hereafter.

After the garden owners' refusal to admit the poor and the loss of their crop, this ayah says that worldly punishment is followed by greater punishment in the Hereafter, completing the consequence of withholding the harvest's share.
The section follows cultivated yield from growth to a harvest share; this ayah says the two gardens gave their produce without failing and had a river between them, staging productive abundance.
The garden owner enters his productive garden while wronging himself; this ayah begins the contrast between a crop's visible abundance and the owner's false confidence that it will last.
The owner says he does not think his garden will ever perish; this claim directly tests the section's distinction between temporary worldly yield and what truly remains.
The section contrasts fields that endure with growth that is lost; this ayah warns that the garden can be struck from heaven and left barren, reversing its earlier abundance.
This continuation says the garden's water could sink into the earth beyond recovery, specifying another way its cultivated yield can fail.
This ayah says the garden's fruits were destroyed and its owner wrung his hands; it completes the reversal from productive garden to lost yield, the opposite of harvest whose due is given.
